subtype: Approach: family conversation about caregiving plans [Action]
passage:
The clinic's waiting room smelled of disinfectant and warm tea. Kashish sat between Papa and Amma, waiting for their routine check-up, while Nikita, Kashish's sister, sat opposite scrolling through her phone. Kashish had been rehearsing this talk for days.
"Amma, Papa, before I go abroad, can we talk about how it will work?"
"We'll manage," Papa said quickly.
"I know. I want to plan, not assume. Nikita is in the same city, so she can handle the visits. I'll come twice a year and phone every Sunday. And if there's an emergency, I'll keep money aside for a flight."
Amma's eyes filled. "We don't want to stand in your way."
"You're not," Kashish said. "This is so I can go without worrying."

qa.q: How often did Kashish plan to phone?
qa.a: Kashish planned to phone every Sunday.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling while rehearsing the talk?
qa.a: Kashish was nervous and caring, rehearsing for days to raise it without hurting them.

qa.q: What could the family add to the plan if a parent's health changes?
qa.a: They could agree in advance who talks to the doctor, and update the plan together on a fixed date.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt hearing the plan?
qa.a: Amma was moved and a little sad, seen in the eyes filling, but also relieved that they would not stand in the way.

grounding: The passage shows a person sitting with parents to discuss visits, emergency travel and support if health worsens, making a plan instead of assuming things will work out.

passage:
Dear Preeti,
You missed Sunday's talk because of your exams, so here's what we decided, before Mummy tells you a dramatic version.
I told Mummy and Papa plainly: if I take the Toronto job, I don't want us to just hope everything works out. So we sat at the dining table with tea and a notebook.
Visits: I'll come home every December, and they'll come for two months once Papa retires.
Emergencies: I'll keep money aside just for a last-minute ticket, and Mama-ji in Nagpur agreed to be the first person to reach them in any crisis.
Health: if Papa's sugar gets worse, we'll talk again about whether I stay abroad at all. Nothing is locked.
Papa cried a little. Then he asked for a second cup of tea.
Your part: you're the one nearby. We'll talk about that too, and it won't all fall on you.
Gargi

qa.q: Who agreed to be the first person to reach Mummy and Papa in a crisis?
What does Papa crying a little and then asking for tea suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Papa felt sad and moved about the move, but also comforted that there was a real plan.

qa.q: What else could the family add to the plan?
qa.a: They could keep key phone numbers and documents in one place and agree how often to check in, so the plan still works on a bad day.

qa.q: How might Preeti read the last part of the letter?
qa.a: Preeti may feel relieved that Gargi sees how much could fall on the sibling nearby and promises it won't all land there.

grounding: It shows someone sitting with parents to plan visits, emergency travel and support if health worsens before deciding to migrate.

subtype: Approach: family conversation about caregiving plans [Action]
passage: Harsha, you asked on your podcast what the hardest part of deciding to move was. It wasn't the visa. It was one Sunday lunch. I'm Zubin, the only child, and my parents are both over sixty. So instead of announcing 'I got the job in Sydney', I asked them to sit with me after the dhansak. I said, let's plan this like a project. Who visits whom, and how often? Mum said she wanted one long visit a year, not three short ones. What if something happens at night? We agreed on our neighbour, Mrs Engineer, and my cousin in Dadar as the first people to call, with both numbers on the fridge. And if Dad's heart gets worse? Then I come back for a stretch, and we decide again together. It wasn't easy. But nobody felt left out of their own future.

qa.q: Who are the first people to call if something happens at night?
qa.a: Their neighbour, Mrs Engineer, and Zubin's cousin in Dadar.

qa.q: What does Zubin mean by 'nobody felt left out of their own future'?
qa.a: Zubin feels relieved and respected that the parents helped make the plan instead of simply being told about the move.

qa.q: What else could Zubin do to keep the plan working after the move?
qa.a: Zubin could set a regular time to review the plan with the parents, perhaps during the long yearly visit, and update it as health changes.

qa.q: How might Zubin's mother see being asked about visits?
qa.a: Being asked lets her choose one long visit a year, so she likely feels respected rather than left behind.

grounding: It shows someone sitting with parents to discuss visits, night emergencies and who helps if health worsens, building a plan together before moving.
